paragraphs: The message arrived while she was deciding where a nail should go.

Aarna had taped a sheet of paper to the living-room wall and drawn a cross at its centre. The afternoon light reached this wall for a little over an hour. She had moved a chair, wiped the paintwork and found the hammer behind a box of winter clothes.
Room Enough waited against the sofa. A blue room, a pale doorway, three uneven marks left by an old coat hook. She wanted one good photograph before it went to the gallery.
Her phone lit up on the chair.
The gallery's message began with an apology. Their funding had fallen through. The exhibition could not proceed. There was no replacement date they could offer.
She read the last sentence, then went back to the first.
On the phone, the coordinator said the decision had come that morning. It was not a judgement on the work.
"But the invitations have gone out."
"I know. I'm sorry."
Aarna looked at the spare copies. Her father had asked for a larger file so he could print one for the shop window. She had sent it before lunch.
"All of them," she said.
She could hear someone typing at the other end of the call. She asked whether she would receive written confirmation, although the message was still open on her screen.

Afterwards she entered CANCELED beside the transport booking in her spreadsheet. She called the driver before the deposit became non-refundable. He asked for the booking number; she found it. He read back the amount; she corrected him.
When the call ended, her palm was wet around the phone.
The cross waited on the wall. She had measured twice. She picked up the hammer, then set it on the chair.
She sat on the floor and turned the painting towards her.

The room belonged to her first Chicago rental. She had kept her paints in a suitcase under the bed. When someone visited, she cleared the table, washed the mugs and pushed the suitcase far enough back that its handle did not show.
The doorway had been narrower than this. She had widened it each time she returned to the canvas. The coat-hook marks stayed where they were.
Her phone chimed with a message from New Jersey. A photograph: her invitation in the shop window, between a guitar and a handwritten sign about lessons.
She enlarged it. Her father had straightened the paper with two strips of tape.
She began typing, "Please take it down."
Then she deleted the words and locked the phone.
For several minutes she studied the place where the pale doorway met the blue. Yesterday she had liked that part.
When she opened Mukund's messages, his latest photograph was still there: the mark on his cuff beside a paper cup of coffee. "Still a limited edition."
She typed an explanation and erased it.
"The show is canceled. Can you come when you're done?"
His reply arrived before the screen dimmed.
"Leaving now."
She put the phone beside her, face up this time.
